title: The De Rham Theorem and Degree

items.title: Standard orientation of the affine simplex
items.statement: The ordered vertices orient Δ^k, and the induced orientation on the ith face is (-1)^i times the orientation from its ordered remaining vertices.
items.strategy: Compute the vertex-permutation determinant, the outward -E_i face wedges and the outward E_1 wedge for face zero. Treat zero-dimensional boundary faces by determinant-line signs while retaining the unique ordering orientation of an abstract point.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Integral of a form over a smooth singular simplex
items.statement: For a smooth singular k-simplex σ and k-form ω near its image, define ∫_σ ω=∫_{Δ^k}σ*ω; in degree zero this is evaluation at σ(v_0).
items.strategy: Prove T_k compact Jordan by the solid-under-a-continuous-graph induction. Integrate its continuous pullback coefficient; compare extensions on the dense interior and extend equality to the boundary. Positive-coordinate independence follows in the stated justification.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Simplex integrals are independent of affine coordinate identification
items.statement: The integral in the preceding definition is unchanged by replacing one orientation-preserving affine identification of aff(Δ^k) with another.
items.strategy: Write h=a^{-1}b and compute the coefficient f(h)det Dh by alternating evaluation. Apply compact-Jordan change of variables, using positivity to identify determinant and absolute determinant; handle k=0 by evaluation.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Stokes theorem for the standard simplex
items.statement: For k≥1 and a smooth (k-1)-form η near Δ^k, ∫_{Δ^k}dη=Σ_i(-1)^i∫_{Δ^{k-1}}δ_i*η.
items.strategy: Expand eta as sum (-1)^(i-1)f_i dx_omit_i. Integrate partial_i f_i by Jordan sections and FTC. Compute every lower-face sign and the face-zero determinant to identify upper endpoint terms. Treat k=1 directly.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Stokes theorem for smooth singular chains
items.statement: For every finite smooth singular chain c and differential form ω of matching degree, ∫_c dω=∫_{∂c}ω.
items.strategy: Apply simplex Stokes on one smooth neighbourhood extension, using derivative and face pullback naturality. Define chain integration on finite coefficient support and explicitly collect repeated faces in the boundary sum.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The de Rham complex and pullback extend to manifolds with boundary
items.statement: Locally extendible boundary-chart coefficients define a chart-independent de Rham complex, with d squared zero, the graded Leibniz rule and natural wedge-preserving pullback, without choice.
items.strategy: Extend finitely many coefficients at one point, use equality of all boundary jets for independence, transfer coordinate naturality to glue d, and restrict d squared zero and Leibniz. Extend the coordinate map before restriction to handle maps wholly into a target boundary. Compute induced quotient maps.

references.title: Ioan Mărcuț, Manifolds (2017 lecture notes), boundary smoothness and forms
John M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Chapters 16–17

items.title: De Rham integration cochain
items.statement: Define I_M(ω)(σ)=∫_σ ω and extend linearly to smooth singular chains.
items.strategy: Extend the uniquely determined simplex values by finite coefficient sums to the supplied free chain space. Prove linearity in forms using coefficient integrals, and retain zero/negative degrees and boundary conventions.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: De Rham integration is a cochain map
items.statement: For every form ω, δI_M(ω)=I_M(dω).
items.strategy: Evaluate the two cochains on an arbitrary finite chain and substitute chain Stokes with the exact unsigned precomposition definition of delta. Treat top form degree and negative degrees without discarding higher singular simplices.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The de Rham map on cohomology is well defined
items.statement: Integration induces I_M:H^k_dR(M)→H^k_{sing,∞}(M;R) in every degree.
items.strategy: Compute delta I(omega)=0 for closed omega and I(omega+d eta)-I(omega)=delta I(eta). Reindex both cochain complexes at n=-k and apply the exact induced-homology theorem, then verify linearity and boundary/degree conventions.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Naturality of the de Rham map
items.statement: For every smooth F:M→N, I_M∘F*=F*∘I_N on forms, cochains, and cohomology.
items.strategy: Use one neighbourhood extension to identify sigma^*F^*omega with (F sigma)^*omega, hence the identical affine integrands. Extend to finite chains and pass to classes, explicitly comparing both changed-representative routes.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The de Rham homotopy formula extends to boundary manifolds
items.statement: The interval contraction of a locally smooth homotopy between manifolds with boundary is a smooth form and satisfies H_1^*-H_0^*=dL_H+L_Hd, without choice.
items.strategy: At one fixed spatial point, use all admissible local extension intervals, a finite subcover and explicit time cutoffs to obtain coefficient extensions across the whole compact parameter interval. Differentiate their integrals and compute d(alpha+dt wedge beta), then descend the endpoint identity to cohomology.

references.title: Nigel Hitchin, Differentiable Manifolds (2014), de Rham homotopy operator

items.title: The de Rham map is an isomorphism on convex coordinate domains
items.statement: On a nonempty convex Euclidean coordinate domain, including a convex relatively open half-space domain arising at a boundary chart, the de Rham map is an isomorphism in all degrees.
items.strategy: Contract by the affine radial homotopy. Use the boundary form operator for primitives and the time-flattened smooth prism for cochains. Compute the full unnormalized point cochain complex, give explicit cocycle primitives, and check integration sends constants identically before transporting by a chart.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: De Rham Mayer–Vietoris with boundary and an explicit partition lift
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, the boundary-compatible de Rham two-open sequence is short exact with V-U difference and positive lift-differential connector; with a supplied partition it is choice-free.
items.strategy: Group a supplied subordinate partition with closed supports; prove injectivity/gluing and the lift (-rho_V eta,rho_U eta), with smooth zero extension. Apply the cohomology LES, compute the positive lift-differential connector and its representative/lift independence, and prove ordered-cover naturality.

references.title: John M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Theorem 17.20

items.title: The de Rham and smooth singular Mayer–Vietoris diagram commutes away from connectors
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, for an ordered cover M=U∪V, the restriction and difference squares in the two Mayer–Vietoris sequences commute with de Rham integration.
items.strategy: Apply cochain naturality to the four open inclusions, compute second-minus-first using real linearity, and identify the first small-complex term by its actual inclusion. Descend the two componentwise identities to cohomology.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The de Rham map commutes with Mayer–Vietoris connectors
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω and the common ordered-cover sign convention, integration intertwines the de Rham and smooth-singular Mayer–Vietoris connecting homomorphisms.
items.strategy: Compare the integrated partition lift e with the explicit singular lift e0=(-E_U c,0). Give the priority-U small cochain t with a(t)=e-e0 and compute delta t=j^*I(zeta)-z0. Use the actual smooth subdivision retraction R and homotopy D to print the full coboundary I(zeta)-R^*z0=delta(I(zeta)D+R^*t).

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The de Rham map is an isomorphism on a two-open union
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, if the de Rham map is an isomorphism on U, V, and U∩V, then it is an isomorphism on U∪V.
items.strategy: Display the five consecutive terms centered at H^q(M), identify the exact three ordinary squares and the connector square, verify all four outside vertical isomorphisms including their direct-sum inverses, and apply the module five lemma. Treat q=0 with two zero terms explicitly.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: De Rham theorem for smooth singular cohomology
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, integration is a natural isomorphism H^k_dR(M)≅H^k_{sing,∞}(M;R) for every smooth manifold, including the published boundary variant.
items.strategy: Verify all hypotheses of the two-stage local-to-global theorem: exact and commuting MV rows, boxes/half-boxes and empty case, and countable product compatibility. Supply boundary-form product gluing and explicitly use AC_omega for component primitives and representatives. Apply the established exhaustion-band and chart-open argument without a continuity axiom.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: De Rham vector-space comparison with continuous singular cohomology
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, integration followed by the smooth-to-continuous comparison is a natural linear isomorphism H^k_dR(M)≅H^k_sing(M;R) in every degree.
items.strategy: Define the unique inverse-restriction composite, prove linearity and its inverse, and cancel the injective restriction map in the explicit contravariant naturality square.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: An affine cone homotopy from the diagonal to the front-back shuffle
items.statement: Finite affine cone chains h_n in Delta^n x Delta^n explicitly fill diagonal minus front/back shuffle, compatibly with the alternating face correction.
items.strategy: Fixed affine cone recursion, with explicit cycle obstruction and double-face cancellation, finite unnormalized chains and extension-independent integration.

references.title: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, section 3.2; affine-cone specialization of the diagonal comparison

items.title: Integration over the signed shuffle equals the product of simplex integrals
items.statement: The signed shuffle integrates the external product of two top simplex forms to the product of their integrals; mismatched bidegrees vanish.
items.strategy: Merged cumulative coordinates give the actual finite triangulation; compute determinant sign, Jordan overlaps and Fubini sections, with separate point factors and rank vanishing.

references.title: Local simplex product integration; shuffle convention from Miller Lecture 7

items.title: De Rham integration respects wedge and cup in cohomology
items.statement: For closed forms α,β, the smooth singular cocycles I(α∧β) and I(α)∪I(β) differ by a coboundary, naturally in the manifold.
items.strategy: Define K on each simplex by integrating the external pulled-back form on the fixed affine cone chain h. The diagonal integral is wedge, the front/back shuffle integral is cup by the proved product calculation. Integrate the chain homotopy and apply simplex Stokes to derive all three terms with their signs. Prove extension independence, naturality, degree-zero normalization and quotient descent.

references.title: Joel W. Robbin, The de Rham Theorem

items.title: The de Rham theorem
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, integration followed by smooth/continuous comparison is a natural graded-algebra isomorphism H*_dR(M)≅H*_{sing}(M;R) for every smooth manifold.
items.strategy: Extend the source quotient algebra to the boundary convention, prove that actual restriction preserves cup and unit on cochains, then cancel restriction in the multiplicativity and unit equations for J=r^{-1}I. Direct-sum degreewise inverse and smooth-map naturality complete the graded-algebra isomorphism; AC_omega is confined to vector-space bijectivity.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem
Joel W. Robbin, The de Rham Theorem

items.title: De Rham cohomology depends only on the underlying homotopy type
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, homeomorphic or homotopy-equivalent underlying spaces have isomorphic real de Rham cohomology groups; for smooth homotopies this agrees with the direct de Rham homotopy operator.
items.strategy: Conjugate the supplied continuous homotopy-inverse pullbacks by J, calculate both inverse composites, and use smooth naturality to identify T_f with ordinary form pullback. The boundary homotopy operator gives the same endpoint equality on closed forms.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The ring form of de Rham’s theorem needs the singular cup product
items.statement: The vector-space comparison alone does not imply multiplicativity; the ring form uses the exact AT-7 cup convention and the explicit wedge–cup comparison homotopy, with no compactness hypothesis.
items.strategy: Exhibit a linear bijection of R failing product and unit, then identify the actual cochain-homotopy, restriction and vertex-unit equations that prove the ring comparison.

references.title: Joel W. Robbin, The de Rham Theorem

items.title: Compactly supported de Rham cohomology
items.statement: Because supp(dω)⊆supp(ω), compactly supported forms form a subcomplex Ω_c^•(M); define H_c^k(M) as its cohomology.
items.strategy: Prove vector-subspace support containment with finite ambient-cover compactness arguments; locality gives supp(d omega) contained in supp omega. Restrict d^2=0, form the quotient and check compact primitives, endpoints and agreement on compact manifolds.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Proper smooth maps pull back compactly supported forms
items.statement: If F:M→N is smooth and proper, meaning that inverse images of compact sets are compact, then F* sends Ω_c^k(N) to Ω_c^k(M).
items.strategy: Use continuity and the pointwise pullback formula to place its nonzero locus in the closed inverse image of the support, then take closure. Properness and an explicit augmented finite-cover argument prove compactness, with linearity inherited.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Compactly supported de Rham cohomology is contravariant for proper smooth maps
items.statement: Proper smooth maps induce contravariant maps on compactly supported de Rham cohomology, compatible with identities and composition.
items.strategy: Check closedness and representative changes with a pulled-back compact primitive, then properness of identities/composites and the actual contravariant equations. The forget-support square is the equality of the same form class.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Finite chart localization gives choice-free integration and compact Stokes
items.statement: On an oriented boundaryless manifold, finite compactly supported chart cutoffs near one compact support define an independent linear local integral, with zero integral on derivatives of compactly supported primitives, without choice.
items.strategy: Construct finite compact chart cutoffs by the full compact-bump construction and a finite all-tuples cover. Establish chart invariance directly on a boundaryless overlap and finite double-sum independence, then linearity/locality and FTC/Fubini compact Stokes.

references.title: Robbin-Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology, section5.2.2 Lemma5.2.10 and section5.2.3 Theorem5.2.12; finite-support specialization

items.title: Integration descends to compactly supported top de Rham cohomology
items.statement: On an oriented boundaryless n-manifold, integration induces a linear map H_c^n(M)→R.
items.strategy: Use the new choice-free finite integral and compact Stokes to annihilate compact boundaries, checking n0 separately and quotient linearity. Only under AC_omega compare a supplied global partition via its finite nonzero products and chart agreement; do not import that axiom into the main result.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Zero-integral compactly supported top forms on Euclidean space have compactly supported primitives
items.statement: If ω∈Ω_c^n(R^n) and ∫ω=0, there is η∈Ω_c^{n-1}(R^n) with dη=ω; the n=0 case is interpreted separately.
items.strategy: Induct with f0(x)=integral f(x,t)dt, normalized bump b, h=integral(f-f0 b), and eta=(-1)^(n-1)h dxprime+gamma wedge b dt. Verify all joint smoothness by parameter integration, exact derivative signs, vanishing support boxes, Fubini zero integral for f0 and n0/n1 separately.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Compactly supported top cohomology propagates across overlapping oriented coordinate balls
items.statement: Let $M^n$ be an oriented smooth manifold without boundary. A coordinate ball here is a domain with a chart onto an open Euclidean ball (or onto $\mathbb R^n$), with the induced orientation. If $U,V$ are such domains with $U\cap V\ne\varnothing$, and $\mu_U,\mu_V\in\Omega_c^n(M)$ have supports compactly contained in $U,V$ respectively and satisfy $\int_M\mu_U=\int_M\mu_V=1$, then $[\mu_U]=[\mu_V]$ in $H_c^n(M)$. Such normalized bump forms exist in every nonempty coordinate ball, and in every nonempty open overlap. Every compactly supported top form whose support is contained in one coordinate ball and whose integral is zero has a compactly supported primitive in that ball; extending the primitive by zero gives an ambient primitive. All integrals are the finite-localization integrals, and no choice axiom is used.
items.strategy: Reparametrize every ball onto all Euclidean space by an explicit radial diffeomorphism, transfer a compact primitive and justify zero extension. Normalize a bump in the overlap by a positive cube integral bound and subtract it from both supplied normalized forms.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Integration is an isomorphism on top compactly supported de Rham cohomology
items.statement: Let $M^n$ be a nonempty connected oriented smooth manifold without boundary. With the finite-localization integral, the map $\operatorname{Int}_M:H_c^n(M)\to\mathbb R$, $[\omega]\mapsto\int_M\omega$, is an isomorphism. More explicitly, a compactly supported top form has integral zero if and only if it is the derivative of a compactly supported $(n-1)$-form. For $n=0$ this means that the zero form has the zero negative-degree primitive. The theorem holds in ZF, without a choice axiom.
items.strategy: Finite-overlap reachability is a nonempty clopen union of chart balls. Finite localization of the one input gives chart terms; subtract each integral times a normalized bump and use local compact primitives. Transport finitely many masses to one base bump along finite overlap chains. Compute the inverse a->[a nu0] and both zero-integral/exact implications in ZF.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Top de Rham cohomology of a closed connected oriented manifold is real
items.statement: For a nonempty closed connected oriented smooth $n$-manifold $M$, where closed means compact and without boundary, integration identifies $H_{\mathrm{dR}}^n(M)$ with $\mathbb R$. The integral is the finite-localization integral, and this assertion is choice-free, including dimension zero.
items.strategy: Identify ordinary and compact-support forms and primitive spaces using compactness, then apply the proved choice-free top compact-support integration isomorphism.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree of a proper smooth map by compact-support cohomology
items.statement:
Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be proper and smooth, with $M,N$ nonempty connected oriented smooth manifolds without boundary. Its **degree** is the scalar
$$\deg(F)=\bigl(\operatorname{Int}_M\circ F_c^*\circ\operatorname{Int}_N^{-1}\bigr)(1)\in\mathbb R,$$
where the integration isomorphisms use the choice-free finite-localization integral. Equivalently, it is the unique scalar satisfying
$$\int_M F^*\omega=\deg(F)\int_N\omega\qquad(\omega\in\Omega_c^n(N)).$$
Integer-valuedness and comparison with the homological degree on closed manifolds are subsequent assertions, not part of this definition's justification.
items.strategy: Define the scalar as L(1) for the actual composite of integration inverse, compact-support pullback and integration; prove inverse linearity by injectivity and the scalar characterization by L(t)=tL(1).

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree is well defined and independent of the normalized top form
items.statement:
For a proper smooth map $F:M^n	o N^n$ between nonempty connected oriented smooth boundaryless manifolds, the scalar in the degree definition exists uniquely. Every $
u\in\Omega_c^n(N)$ with $\int_N
u=1$ satisfies $\deg(F)=\int_MF^*
u$. This value is independent of the normalized form, and for every compactly supported top form $\omega$ it satisfies $\int_MF^*\omega=\deg(F)\int_N\omega$. All assertions are choice-free.
items.strategy: Subtract a times one normalized top form, where a is the input integral. Pull back its actual compact primitive using properness, apply compact Stokes and then evaluate on each normalized form for independence and uniqueness.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Local orientation sign of a regular preimage
items.statement: Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be a smooth map of oriented smooth manifolds, and let $p$ be a regular preimage of $y$, so $F(p)=y$ and $dF_p:T_pM\to T_yN$ is an isomorphism. The **local orientation sign** $\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)$ is $+1$ if the induced isomorphism of determinant lines carries the chosen ray of $T_pM$ to the chosen ray of $T_yN$, and $-1$ if it carries it to the other ray. For $n>0$ it is the sign of the derivative determinant in positively oriented bases. For $n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_M(p)\varepsilon_N(y)$, comparing the two specified rays directly; it need not be $+1$, although the empty determinant is one.
items.strategy: Compare determinant-line rays intrinsically, verify positive-coordinate determinant sign by Q^-1AP, and compute zero-dimensional sign from the two supplied point signs rather than the empty determinant.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Regular-value formula for compact-support degree
items.statement:
Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be a proper smooth map between nonempty connected oriented smooth manifolds without boundary. If $y\in N$ is a regular value, then its fibre is finite and
$$\deg(F)=\sum_{p\in F^{-1}(y)}\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)\in\mathbb Z.$$
An empty fibre gives the empty sum zero. In dimension zero the signs compare the supplied determinant-line rays. The formula is choice-free and presupposes only a given regular value, not a theorem asserting their existence.
items.strategy: Compact fibre plus all isolating inverse neighbourhoods gives finiteness without choosing infinitely many branches. Disjoint finitely many branches and the compact set C=F^-1(K) minus their union give a target ball with no extra preimages. Normalize one bump, split its pullback into compact zero-extended branch forms and evaluate them in the pulled-back target chart with each signed orientation. Handle empty fibre and n0 directly.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Smooth orientation sign is the local integral homology multiplier
items.statement:
Fix a dimension $n\ge1$ and one generator $e_n$ of $H_n(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\};\mathbb Z)$. A smooth orientation on a boundaryless $n$-manifold determines an integral local-homology orientation by requiring each positive chart centred at $p$ to send its local generator $\mu_p$ to $e_n$. This is independent of the positive chart and is a continuous generator section of the orientation local system. Use the same $e_n$ for all manifolds being compared.

If $F$ is smooth near $p$, $F(p)=q$, and $dF_p$ is invertible, its induced map on local integral homology carries $\mu_p$ to $\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)\mu_q$. In dimension zero put $e_0=[\mathrm{point}]$; the smooth sign $\varepsilon(p)$ gives $\mu_p=\varepsilon(p)[p]$, and the local multiplier is the product of the source and target point signs. All assertions are choice-free. The local map is formed on a sufficiently small neighbourhood on which $p$ is the only preimage of $q$.
items.strategy: Compute local reflection action through the pair sequence and reduced sphere homology, then use elementary factorization with explicit shear/positive-scale homotopies and swap conjugacy. Compare a differentiable germ with its derivative by a nonzero remainder homotopy. Prove chart independence and closed-ball section continuity of the smooth-induced integral orientation, including dimension zero.

references.title: Alexander Kupers, Algebraic Topology, section8.1 pp60–62; local degree and regular-value computation

items.title: Regular-value formula for degree
items.statement:
Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be proper and smooth between nonempty connected oriented smooth manifolds without boundary, and let $y\in N$ be a regular value. Then the fibre is finite and
$$\deg(F)=\sum_{p\in F^{-1}(y)}\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)\in\mathbb Z.$$
If $M,N$ are closed, this scalar is also their integral homological degree: with the integral orientations induced by the supplied smooth orientations using the same Euclidean generator convention,
$$F_*[M]=\deg(F)[N]\quad\text{in }H_n(N;\mathbb Z).$$
The formula includes the empty regular fibre and dimension zero. This comparison at a supplied regular value is choice-free; it does not assert existence of regular values as an additional premise-free conclusion.
items.strategy: Use the completed proper signed-count theorem and compute closed-manifold homological degree independently by finite-puncture excision: the fundamental class restricts to the tuple of local orientation generators, whose germ images are determinant signs times the target generator. The quotient-chain square gives equality; empty fibre factors through the punctured target and n0 is a signed point.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree is an integer and independent of the regular value
items.statement: Every regular fibre gives the same integer signed count, namely the compact-support degree.
items.strategy: Apply the formula to any regular value; the left-hand degree was defined independently of a value.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree is multiplicative under composition
items.statement: For composable proper smooth maps between connected oriented n-manifolds, deg(G∘F)=deg(F)deg(G); on closed manifolds this agrees with AT-8 functoriality.
items.strategy: Evaluate (G∘F)*=F*G* on a normalized compactly supported top form and apply the defining scalar twice; identify the closed restriction using the AT-8 comparison.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree of an orientation-preserving or reversing diffeomorphism
items.statement: An orientation-preserving diffeomorphism has degree +1 and an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism has degree -1.
items.strategy: Diffeomorphisms are proper and oriented change of variables gives the defining integral identity with the appropriate sign.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree is invariant under proper smooth homotopy
items.statement: If H:M×[0,1]→N is a proper smooth homotopy between proper maps F_0,F_1, then deg(F_0)=deg(F_1). Proper endpoints alone do not suffice.
items.strategy: For compactly supported top ω, use the standard interval homotopy formula F_1*ω-F_0*ω=dKω; properness of H keeps Kω compactly supported, so its integral vanishes.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: A nonzero-degree map to a connected manifold is surjective
items.statement: A proper smooth same-dimensional map of nonzero degree to a connected oriented target is surjective.
items.strategy: First prove a proper map between manifolds is closed: intersect with a relatively compact target neighborhood, use compact inverse image, and project its closed compact image. If y is missed, choose a normalized compactly supported top form in a coordinate ball disjoint from that closed image; its pullback is zero, forcing degree zero.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree of the antipodal map on the sphere
items.statement: For n≥1, the antipodal map on oriented S^n has degree (-1)^{n+1}.
items.strategy: Compare the boundary orientation at x and -x: the ambient derivative has determinant (-1)^{n+1} after accounting for the reversed outward normal; then use the diffeomorphism degree.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree of the power map on the circle
items.statement: For every integer m, z↦z^m on the oriented circle has degree m.
items.strategy: Use [0] as a regular value when m is nonzero: its |m| explicitly listed preimages all have derivative sign sgn(m). For m=0 use the empty regular fibre over [1/2]. Verify properness from compactness of the quotient circle.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: The de Rham map is a cochain map without Stokes on simplices
items.statement: False: simplex Stokes is exactly the identity δI=Id.
items.strategy: Evaluate on one simplex to expose the equivalence, so omitting simplex Stokes leaves the cochain claim unproved.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Naturality alone gives Mayer–Vietoris connector compatibility
items.statement: False: ordinary restriction naturality does not by itself identify the lift-differential definitions of two connecting maps.
items.strategy: On the two-arc circle cover with nonzero degree-zero connector, use the degreewise natural family T^q=(-1)^q id. It commutes with every restriction but anticommutes with the nonzero connector. Then identify the explicit lift comparison needed for the genuine integration map.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The vector-space de Rham comparison is automatically a ring isomorphism
items.statement: False: a vector-space comparison need not preserve products; wedge–cup compatibility is an additional cochain-homotopy obligation.
items.strategy: Contrast the linear Mayer–Vietoris proof with the separate multiplicativity identity.

references.title: Joel W. Robbin, The de Rham Theorem

items.title: Compactly supported cohomology is contravariant for every smooth map
items.statement: False: pullback need not preserve compact support unless an appropriate properness condition holds.
items.strategy: Use a constant form supported near a point and a nonproper constant map whose inverse image of that support is noncompact.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree is the unsigned number of points in a regular fibre
items.statement: False: degree is the signed sum of local orientation signs.
items.strategy: Use the proper map x↦x² on oriented real lines. The regular fibre over 1 is {-1,1}, with derivative signs -1 and +1, so its unsigned count is two and its degree is zero.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: A homotopy between proper maps is automatically proper
items.statement: False: properness of the combined map M×[0,1]→N is an extra hypothesis.
items.strategy: Use H(x,t)=(2t-1)^2x. Both endpoint maps are the identity, but the inverse image of the compact singleton {0} contains the noncompact slice R×{1/2}.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

title: The De Rham Theorem and Degree — Examples

items.title: De Rham integration cochain on a smooth path
items.statement: For σ:[0,1]→M and a one-form ω, I(ω)(σ)=∫_0^1ω_{σ(t)}(σ'(t))dt.
items.strategy: Pull back the form to the standard one-simplex and write its coefficient.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Chain Stokes on an oriented two-simplex
items.statement: For an oriented smooth two-simplex, the integral of dη equals the alternating integral over its three oriented edges.
items.strategy: Expand ∂[v_0v_1v_2]=[v_1v_2]-[v_0v_2]+[v_0v_1] and apply chain Stokes.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The de Rham map on the angular form
items.statement: The normalized angular one-form integrates to one on the positively oriented generator of S^1.
items.strategy: Parametrize the circle once and compute the pullback dθ/(2π).

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: The local de Rham comparison on a ball
items.statement: On a Euclidean ball, the de Rham map is identity on constants and both sides vanish in positive degree.
items.strategy: Display the radial contraction for forms and the affine prism for smooth singular chains.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: Connector compatibility for a two-arc cover of the circle
items.statement: For a two-arc cover of S^1, the signed overlap zero-cocycle and partition lift map to the same generator under the two connectors.
items.strategy: Choose ordered arcs, write the V-U overlap values and compute the positive lift differential on both sides.

references.title: Peter S. Park, Proof of de Rham's Theorem

items.title: A normalized compactly supported top form on Euclidean space
items.statement: A product of normalized one-variable smooth bumps times dx_1∧…∧dx_n is a compactly supported top form of integral one.
items.strategy: Use Fubini for the product coefficient and the standard orientation.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree of a reflection of a sphere
items.statement: Reflection in one ambient coordinate restricts to an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism of S^n and has degree -1.
items.strategy: Compare outward-normal-first oriented bases and apply the diffeomorphism formula.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Degree of z to the m on the circle from a regular value
items.statement: For m≠0 every regular value of z↦z^m has |m| preimages, all with sign sgn(m), so the signed count is m.
items.strategy: List the lifted angles and differentiate θ↦mθ.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: A displayed two-sheeted orientation-preserving covering has degree two
items.statement: For the displayed proper local diffeomorphism with exactly two orientation-preserving sheets, every fibre contributes +1+1 and the degree is two.
items.strategy: Verify directly for this map that the two inverse branches are orientation preserving; no general covering theorem is used.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: A map with two preimages but degree zero
items.statement: The smooth proper map F:S^1→S^1 given by F(e^{iθ})=e^{i sin θ} has the regular value 1 with exactly two preimages and opposite local signs, hence degree zero.
items.strategy: The equation sin θ=0 modulo 2π has exactly θ=0,π because sin θ∈[-1,1]. In oriented angular coordinates the derivative is cos θ, giving signs +1 and -1; compactness makes F proper.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Proper endpoint maps joined by a nonproper combined homotopy
items.statement: There are proper smooth maps F_0,F_1:R→R and a smooth homotopy H between them whose combined map R×[0,1]→R is not proper.
items.strategy: Take H(x,t)=(2t-1)^2x on R×[0,1]. Both endpoint maps are the identity and hence proper, but H^{-1}({0}) contains the noncompact set R×{1/2}, so the combined homotopy is not proper.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

items.title: Nonzero degree forces surjectivity on closed oriented manifolds
items.statement: A closed oriented same-dimensional map computed to have nonzero degree cannot omit any target point.
items.strategy: If a target point is omitted, the image of a source fundamental cycle vanishes in relative homology at that point; the homological degree equation and the target local orientation generator then force degree zero.

references.title: Robbin–Salamon, Introduction to Differential Topology

title: Geodesics the Exponential Map Completeness and Hopf Rinow

items.title: Boundaryless convention for geodesic flow and Hopf–Rinow
items.statement: Throughout this page, geodesic flow, exponential maps, geodesic completeness, and Hopf–Rinow are asserted for smooth manifolds without boundary. Metric statements explicitly about an embedded submanifold may still allow boundary. Without this convention a compact interval is metric-complete but its outward geodesics have no two-sided continuation inside the interval.
items.strategy: Record the scope convention before the geodesic definition; boundary variants require inward/tangent initial data, doubling, or a different completeness notion and are not silently inferred.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Lectures 15.1 and 19.2, pp.113 and 141–144
Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness

items.title: Geodesic of an affine connection
items.statement: On a smooth manifold without boundary, a smooth curve γ is an affinely parametrized geodesic when D_tγ'=0.
items.strategy: Use the intrinsic covariant derivative along a curve; constant curves are included.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Geodesics have constant speed for a metric-compatible connection
items.statement: For a metric-compatible connection, g(γ',γ') is constant along every geodesic.
items.strategy: Differentiate the squared speed using metric compatibility and substitute D_tγ'=0.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Coordinate geodesic equation
items.statement: In coordinates a curve is geodesic iff x¨^k+Γ^k_{ij}(x)x˙^i x˙^j=0 for every k.
items.strategy: Expand D_t(x˙^j∂_j) with the connection Leibniz rule.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Geodesic spray
items.statement: The geodesic spray on TM has local expression v^i∂_{x^i}-Γ^k_{ij}(x)v^iv^j∂_{v^k}.
items.strategy: Define it in induced tangent-bundle coordinates; coordinate independence is the next obligation.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: The geodesic spray is a well-defined smooth vector field on TM
items.statement: The local spray formulas agree on overlaps and define a smooth vector field whose integral curves are exactly velocity lifts of geodesics.
items.strategy: Differentiate the tangent-coordinate transformation, insert the Christoffel transformation law, and identify the resulting first-order system with the intrinsic geodesic equation.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Existence uniqueness and smooth dependence of geodesics
items.statement: For every (p,v)∈TM there is a unique maximal geodesic γ_{p,v}, and (t,p,v)↦γ_{p,v}(t) is smooth on an open domain.
items.strategy: Apply the maximal-flow theorem to the spray and project its integral curve; the velocity component proves the prescribed initial data and the coordinate equation proves the converse.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Affine reparametrization of a geodesic is a geodesic
items.statement: If γ is geodesic and at+b stays in its domain, t↦γ(at+b) is geodesic; its speed is |a| times the original speed.
items.strategy: Apply the covariant chain rule twice, obtaining D_t(γ∘ℓ)'=a²(D_sγ')∘ℓ.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Geodesic scaling identity
items.statement: γ_{p,av}(t)=γ_{p,v}(at) wherever both sides are defined.
items.strategy: The two curves solve the same initial-value problem at zero, so uniqueness identifies them on the common interval.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Geodesically complete Riemannian manifold
items.statement: A boundaryless Riemannian manifold is geodesically complete when every maximal geodesic is defined on all of R.
items.strategy: Quantify over every initial vector, including zero; componentwise interpretation handles disconnected manifolds.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Domain and exponential map of a connection
items.statement: Let E={v∈TM:1∈I_v}; define exp(v)=γ_v(1) and exp_p as its restriction to E∩T_pM.
items.strategy: Use maximal geodesic domains, so no global completeness is presumed.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: The exponential domain is open and the exponential map is smooth
items.statement: E is open in TM and exp:E→M is smooth.
items.strategy: The spray’s maximal flow domain is open; intersect it with time 1 and project the smooth flow.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: The exponential map scales geodesic time
items.statement: Whenever defined, exp_p(tv)=γ_{p,v}(t).
items.strategy: Apply scaling with γ_{p,tv}(1)=γ_{p,v}(t).

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: The differential of exp at zero is the identity
items.statement: Under T_{0_p}(T_pM)≅T_pM, d(exp_p)_{0_p}=id.
items.strategy: Differentiate s↦exp_p(sw)=γ_{p,w}(s) at s=0.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Choice-free smooth inverse function theorem in Euclidean space
items.statement: In ZF, a smooth map between positive finite-dimensional Euclidean open sets with invertible derivative at a point restricts to a diffeomorphism between neighborhoods of that point and its image.
items.strategy: Normalize the derivative and use the Newton contraction on a closed Euclidean ball. Prove that ball complete directly: a Cauchy sequence converges in Euclidean space and the norm inequality keeps its limit in the ball. Banach iteration gives the unique local inverse without a selection. The estimate makes the inverse continuous; differentiating f(g(y))=y gives Dg=(Df∘g)^{-1}, and induction on derivatives bootstraps g from C1 to smooth.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Existence of normal neighborhoods
items.statement: For every p, exp_p is a diffeomorphism from a star-shaped neighborhood of 0 in T_pM onto a neighborhood of p.
items.strategy: In positive dimension apply the choice-free Euclidean inverse lemma in linear and manifold charts, then shrink the source to a ball contained in the inverse-function neighborhood. In dimension zero the exponential map is locally the identity on the discrete manifold.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Normal neighborhood and normal coordinate chart
items.statement: A normal neighborhood of p is the image under exp_p of a star-shaped zero-neighborhood on which exp_p is a diffeomorphism; a supplied basis of T_pM gives its normal coordinates.
items.strategy: Separate the intrinsic exponential chart from the basis-dependent R^n coordinate representation.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Properties of normal coordinates at the center
items.statement: With an orthonormal starting basis, g_{ij}(p)=δ_{ij}, Γ^k_{ij}(p)=0, and radial coordinate lines are geodesics.
items.strategy: The basis gives the metric value; radial lines follow exponential scaling. Insert all radial initial vectors into the geodesic equation to show the symmetric Christoffel coefficients vanish at p.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Injectivity radius at a point and of a manifold
items.statement: inj(p) is the supremum of r>0 for which exp_p is defined and diffeomorphic on B_r(0); inj(M)=inf_p inj(p).
items.strategy: Allow +∞ for the pointwise supremum and zero for the global infimum.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Injectivity radius at each point is positive
items.statement: Every point has positive injectivity radius, although the global infimum can be zero.
items.strategy: A normal ball supplies a positive admissible radius; the counterexample page treats failure of a uniform lower bound.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Smooth variation and variation field of a curve
items.statement: A smooth variation is a smooth map α:(-ε,ε)×[a,b]→M with α(0,t)=γ(t); V=∂_sα|_0. Fixed-endpoint variations keep both endpoint curves constant.
items.strategy: State separately proper endpoint variations, where endpoint values may move and boundary terms remain.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Energy of a piecewise smooth curve
items.statement: For γ:[a,b]→M piecewise smooth, E(γ)=1/2∫_a^b|γ'|²dt.
items.strategy: Sum the ordinary integrals over any finite smooth subdivision; additivity makes the result subdivision-independent.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Length-energy inequality and equality case
items.statement: L(γ)²≤2(b-a)E(γ), with equality exactly when speed is constant almost everywhere, hence on each smooth piece.
items.strategy: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to |γ'| and 1; characterize equality by proportionality and use continuity on pieces.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: First variation formula for energy
items.statement: For a smooth variation of a smooth curve, dE/ds|_0=g(V,γ')|_a^b-∫_a^b g(V,D_tγ')dt; for piecewise-smooth curves add the signed corner terms.
items.strategy: Differentiate under the integral, use metric compatibility and torsion-free interchange D_s∂_t=D_t∂_s, then integrate by parts on each smooth piece.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Geodesics are exactly critical points of energy with fixed endpoints
items.statement: A smooth curve is geodesic iff every smooth fixed-endpoint variation has zero first energy variation.
items.strategy: One direction kills boundary and integral terms. Conversely, near any parameter value choose a curve chart and a one-variable bump, represent a compactly supported field in that trivialization, and realize it by coordinate addition for sufficiently small variation parameter. Taking the field to be a bumped copy of the covariant acceleration forces that acceleration to vanish pointwise.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: First variation formula for length
items.statement: For a regular central curve, the first length variation equals the endpoint tangential terms minus the integral of V against the covariant derivative of the unit tangent, with corner terms piecewise.
items.strategy: Differentiate |∂_tα|, divide by the nonzero speed, use metric compatibility, and integrate by parts after decomposing acceleration into tangential and normal parts.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Gauss lemma
items.statement: Where exp_p is defined, d(exp_p)_v sends the radial vector v to γ'_{p,v}(1), preserves its squared norm, and makes it orthogonal to images of vectors tangent to the sphere |v|=constant.
items.strategy: Use the two-parameter variation exp_p(t(v+sw)); torsion-free interchange and the geodesic equation show d/dt g(∂_s,∂_t)=1/2∂_s|∂_t|². Constant initial speed makes this zero for w⊥v; integrate from t=0 and handle the radial component separately.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Polar form of the metric in normal coordinates
items.statement: Away from the center of a normal neighborhood, the metric has polar form dr²+g_r with no radial-angular cross terms.
items.strategy: Split each tangent vector into radial and sphere-tangent components and apply Gauss lemma.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Radial geodesics minimize length in a normal neighborhood
items.statement: In a normal ball, the radial geodesic from p to exp_p(v) minimizes length among curves remaining in the ball; equality forces a monotone radial reparametrization.
items.strategy: Write any competitor in polar coordinates. Gauss gives |c'|²=(r')²+|angular|²≥(r')², integrate |r'|≥|Δr|, and analyze equality.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Local distance formula in a normal neighborhood
items.statement: For v in a normal ball, d(p,exp_pv)=|v|; every competitor leaving the normal neighbourhood has strictly greater length.
items.strategy: The radial segment has length |v|; any curve leaving a smaller containing normal ball pays at least its boundary radius, while curves staying inside satisfy radial minimality.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Sufficiently short geodesic segments are uniquely minimizing
items.statement: A geodesic segment lying inside a normal ball with initial velocity shorter than its normal radius is uniquely minimizing there, up to monotone reparametrization; consequently every point has a neighborhood where sufficiently short segments have this property.
items.strategy: Represent the segment radially by exponential scaling. Radial minimality gives the length bound and its equality case; injectivity of the normal chart gives uniqueness.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: Existence of geodesically convex neighborhoods
items.statement: Every point has a sufficiently small strongly convex neighborhood: each two points are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic lying inside and smoothly depending on endpoints, and every piecewise-smooth minimizer has that oriented trace; finite nonempty intersections remain strongly convex.
items.strategy: After Gauss-law radial minimality, apply the inverse theorem to (q,v)↦(q,exp_qv) near the zero section and shrink uniformly in a relatively compact coordinate ball. The resulting endpoint solution stays in the ball and is uniquely minimizing; global uniqueness makes finite nonempty intersections strongly convex.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry
Roland Steinbauer, Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 2.2.7

items.title: Length minimizers are constant-speed geodesics up to reparametrization
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega, a nonconstant length-minimizing piecewise-smooth curve on a boundaryless Riemannian manifold factors through cumulative arclength as a unit-speed geodesic. Its constant-speed representative is smooth and unbroken; any original nonzero one-sided corner velocities have the same positive direction, while zero-speed pauses are collapsed.
items.strategy: Prove every subarc minimizes, factor the curve canonically through cumulative arclength, and show the factor is distance preserving. In a strongly convex neighborhood, minimizer uniqueness identifies each short factor with the affine unit-speed connector; these local representatives make the factor a global geodesic and explicitly classify corners and pauses.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry
Roland Steinbauer, Riemannian Geometry, Remark 2.3.10 and Corollary 2.3.11

items.title: Geodesics continue while velocity lifts remain compact
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega and the boundaryless convention, if the velocity lift (γ,γ') stays in a compact subset of TM along a tail approaching either finite endpoint of its interval, then the geodesic extends past that endpoint. Consequently a maximal geodesic's lift leaves every compact subset along such a tail.
items.strategy: Use openness of the maximal spray-flow domain to index an ambient-open cover by pairs (epsilon,U) with (-epsilon,epsilon)xU in the flow domain. A finite subcover of the compact lift set has a positive minimum time; starting sufficiently near either endpoint and using flow uniqueness gives the extension.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, proof of Proposition 20.2.2, p.151
Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, proof of Theorem 11.5.1, printed pp.106–107

items.title: A finite endpoint of a maximal unit-speed geodesic produces a Cauchy curve
items.statement: A unit-speed geodesic on a nonempty interval with a finite right endpoint is Cauchy in its connected component as t approaches that endpoint: for every epsilon, all sufficiently late pairs have distance below epsilon. The left-endpoint version follows by reversal.
items.strategy: The trace lies in one open connected component. For s<t, distance there is at most the length of the restricted unit-speed segment, namely t-s; choosing T=max(r,b-epsilon/2) proves the exact two-parameter Cauchy condition.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, proof of Theorem 11.5.1, printed p.106

items.title: Metric completeness implies geodesic completeness
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega, a connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold complete for its Riemannian distance is geodesically complete.
items.strategy: Rescale a nonconstant finite-endpoint maximal geodesic to unit speed. An explicit endpoint sequence is Cauchy and converges by metric completeness, and the whole tail has the same limit. In one tangent-bundle chart, local metric comparison bounds the unit velocity coordinates over a compact base ball, so the lift tail lies in a compact subset of TM; compact-lift continuation contradicts maximality.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 19.2.1, implication (1) implies (2), pp.141–142
Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1, implication (1) implies (2), printed pp.106–107

items.title: Radial geodesics from one point reach every point under global exponential domain
items.statement: If exp_p is defined on all T_pM, every q in the connected component of p is joined to p by a minimizing radial geodesic.
items.strategy: For any distinct x,y, minimize distance to y on a sufficiently small normal sphere about x and use a near-minimizing competitor plus its sphere crossing to prove the additive identity d(x,y)=delta+d(z,y). Starting at p, follow the resulting unit ray and let A be the parameters satisfying the additive identity with q. Downward closure and a supremum put T in A; repeating the local sphere step at gamma(T), then applying the exact no-corners theorem to the concatenated global minimizer, extends A beyond T unless T=d(p,q).

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 19.2.1, implication (3) to (5), pp.142--144
Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1, implication (3) to (*p), printed pp.107--108

items.title: Hopf–Rinow theorem
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega, for a nonempty connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold, metric completeness, geodesic completeness, global exp_p for one/every p, and compactness of every closed bounded set are equivalent; under them every two points admit a minimizing geodesic.
items.strategy: Close the exact cycle metric complete => geodesically complete => every exponential fibre global => one fibre global => proper => metric complete. For properness, a bounded set lies in the continuous exponential image of one compact tangent ball and is closed there. For the final implication, place a Cauchy sequence in one compact closed ball and use compact metric spaces are complete. Nonemptiness is explicit because the one-basepoint clause otherwise fails on the empty manifold.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 19.2.1 and proof, pp.141--144
Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1 and proof, printed pp.106--108

items.title: Complete connected Riemannian manifolds are proper length spaces
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega, a nonempty complete connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold is a proper length space: closed bounded sets are compact, its distance is the infimum of Riemannian curve lengths, and that infimum is realized by a minimizing geodesic.
items.strategy: Read properness and minimizing geodesics from Hopf–Rinow and the induced-length-metric clause directly from the definition of Riemannian distance; preserve Hopf–Rinow's nonempty, boundaryless, and AC_omega hypotheses.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 19.2.1 and proof, pp.141--144

items.title: Compact Riemannian manifolds are geodesically complete
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega, every compact boundaryless Riemannian manifold, including the disconnected or empty cases, is geodesically complete; each component is compact and complete for its intrinsic Riemannian distance.
items.strategy: Each component is open, closed and compact; its intrinsic distance induces its manifold topology, so compact metric completeness and Hopf–Rinow apply. Finish with the componentwise definition of geodesic completeness and treat the empty manifold directly.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 19.2.1 and compact-manifold consequence, pp.141--144

items.title: Closed embedded submanifolds of complete Riemannian manifolds are complete
items.statement: A closed embedded submanifold with the induced Riemannian metric is complete when the ambient Riemannian manifold is complete.
items.strategy: The inclusion preserves curve lengths, so intrinsic Cauchy implies ambient Cauchy componentwise. Ambient completeness and closedness give a limit in the embedded submanifold; closedness of the source component plus the subspace and Riemannian-distance topologies put that limit in the same component and give intrinsic convergence without a family of choices.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Section 19.1, pp.139--141

items.title: Local isometries send geodesics to geodesics
items.statement: A local Riemannian isometry intertwines the two Levi-Civita covariant derivatives locally and therefore sends affinely parametrized geodesics to affinely parametrized geodesics.
items.strategy: Restrict to neighborhoods on which the map is an isometry. Pull the target connection back and verify torsion-freeness and metric compatibility; uniqueness of Levi-Civita identifies it with the source connection. Apply this identity to the velocity field along a curve.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: A local isometry from a complete connected manifold has geodesically complete target image
items.statement: Assuming AC_omega, if F:M→N is a local isometry of boundaryless Riemannian manifolds and M is complete and connected, then F(M) is open and geodesically complete; every maximal N-geodesic whose initial basepoint lies in F(M) is global and remains in F(M).
items.strategy: For fixed target initial data choose one source preimage and invert its differential. Hopf–Rinow runs the lifted source geodesic globally; local-isometry preservation and geodesic uniqueness identify its image with both the geodesic in the open image and the maximal target geodesic. No covering-map conclusion is asserted.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Theorem 20.1.1 and geodesic-lifting step, pp.147--149

items.title: A Riemannian product is complete iff each factor is complete
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. For a finite family of nonempty connected boundaryless Riemannian manifolds, with the empty product interpreted as a point, metric completeness of every factor, geodesic completeness of every factor, metric completeness of the product metric and geodesic completeness of the product are equivalent.
items.strategy: The block metric has the factor Christoffel symbols and zero mixed symbols, so the coordinate geodesic equations split. Combine global factor geodesics in one direction and project a global product geodesic with constant auxiliary factors in the other, then use Hopf--Rinow for metric completeness.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 8.2.8, p.49

items.title: Incompleteness is finite-time geodesic escape
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. A connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold is metrically incomplete iff a unit-speed maximal geodesic has a finite endpoint and eventually leaves every compact subset toward that endpoint; on the empty manifold both sides are false.
items.strategy: Use Hopf--Rinow to obtain a nonzero finite-endpoint maximal geodesic and rescale it to unit speed. Prove that unit tangent vectors over a compact base set form a compact subset of TM in finitely many tangent charts, then apply compact velocity-lift escape. The converse follows immediately from the finite maximal endpoint.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1 and proof, printed pp.106--107

items.title: Every affinely reparametrized geodesic remains unit speed
items.statement: False: affine reparametrization preserves the geodesic equation but multiplies speed by the absolute slope.
items.strategy: Apply t↦2t to a unit-speed Euclidean line.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.title: The exponential map is always defined on all of TM
items.statement: False: global exponential domain is equivalent to geodesic completeness on each connected component.
items.strategy: Use a radial geodesic in an open Euclidean ball that reaches the boundary in finite time.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Definition 15.1.1, Example 15.1.3, Definition 17.1.2, and Theorem 19.2.1, pp. 113--114, 127--128, and 141--144

items.title: Normal coordinates make the metric Euclidean throughout the chart
items.statement: False: normal coordinates normalize the metric and Christoffel symbols only at their center.
items.strategy: On the unit two-sphere with the induced metric, verify by tangent projection and Levi-Civita uniqueness that exp_N(x)=(sin r/r)x+(cos r)N for r=|x|. At any 0<r<π, its differential in a direction perpendicular to x has length scale sin(r)/r≠1, so the pullback metric is not Euclidean away from the center; no later curvature theory is used.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 17.1.3, Definition 17.2.1 and Proposition 17.2.2, pp. 128, 130--131

items.title: Every geodesic segment is globally length minimizing
items.statement: False: geodesics minimize only locally before cut phenomena.
items.strategy: On the flat quotient circle R/Z with metric dθ², the coordinate geodesic equation makes every constant-speed lifted angular arc a geodesic. A lift whose change lies strictly between 1/2 and 1 is longer than the complementary lift with the same endpoints.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Corollary 16.4.5 and following counterexample, p. 126; Corollary 18.1.3 and proof, pp. 135--136

items.title: Any two points admit a minimizing geodesic
items.statement: False without completeness.
items.strategy: In R²\{0} with the Euclidean metric, every curve from (-1,0) to (1,0) has length at least the ambient Euclidean distance 2. Detours around the origin have lengths tending to 2, while equality in the integral triangle inequality forces the omitted straight segment, so the infimum is not attained.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1 and proof, printed pp. 106--108

items.title: Geodesic completeness means compactness
items.statement: False: completeness gives compact closed bounded subsets, not compactness of the whole manifold.
items.strategy: Euclidean space is complete and noncompact.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1 and proof, printed pp. 106--108

title: Geodesics the Exponential Map Completeness and Hopf Rinow — Examples

items.title: Straight lines as Euclidean geodesics
items.statement: For the Euclidean metric, geodesics are exactly affine paths p+tv; nonconstant images are straight lines and zero speed gives a constant path.
items.strategy: All Christoffel symbols vanish, so x¨=0.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 15.1.3, p. 114

items.title: Great circles as round-sphere geodesics
items.statement: Nonconstant geodesics of the round sphere trace great circles at constant speed.
items.strategy: For the induced round metric, define ∇_XY as the tangent projection of the ambient derivative and verify directly that it is torsion-free and metric-compatible; Levi-Civita uniqueness identifies it with the intrinsic connection. Thus intrinsic acceleration vanishes exactly when γ'' is normal to the sphere, and constant speed then gives γ''=-c²γ, whose nonconstant solutions trace great circles.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Proposition 15.3.1, pp. 117--118

items.title: Geodesics of a Riemannian product
items.statement: A curve in a Riemannian product is geodesic iff each factor curve is geodesic with the same affine parameter.
items.strategy: Compute the split Levi-Civita connection and set both components of the covariant acceleration to zero.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 8.2.8, p.49

items.title: Geodesics in the Poincare upper half-plane
items.statement: For g=(dx²+dy²)/y², nonconstant geodesics are vertical lines and Euclidean semicircles orthogonal to the boundary, with affine parametrizations; zero-speed curves are constant.
items.strategy: Compute Christoffel symbols, integrate the constants x'/y² and squared speed to exhaust both families, and directly verify their affine parametrizations.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 15.1.6, p. 115

items.title: Normal coordinates on the round sphere
items.statement: At p∈S^n, exp_p(v)=cos|v|p+sin|v|v/|v|, with the continuous value p at v=0; it is injective on |v|<π.
items.strategy: Solve the great-circle initial-value problem and locate the first antipodal collision at radius π.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 17.1.3 and Definition 17.2.1, pp. 128 and 130

items.title: The exponential map of a flat torus is not injective
items.statement: Assuming AC_ω, for n≥1 and a full-rank lattice Λ, the flat torus R^n/Λ has exp_[x](v)=[x+v] on every tangent vector; it is Λ-periodic and noninjective. For n=0 the map is injective.
items.strategy: Descend Euclidean straight lines and compare vectors differing by a lattice vector.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Definition 17.1.2, pp. 127–128

items.title: The punctured Euclidean plane is geodesically incomplete
items.statement: R²\{0} with the Euclidean metric is geodesically incomplete.
items.strategy: Use the restricted Euclidean metric and zero Christoffel symbols; calculate the unit-speed maximal geodesic gamma(t)=(1-t,0) on (-infinity,1), then exclude a time-1 extension through the deleted origin by continuity.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness

items.title: An open Euclidean unit ball is metrically incomplete
items.statement: For n≥1 the open unit ball in R^n with Euclidean distance is incomplete; the zero-dimensional ball is a complete singleton.
items.strategy: A radial sequence approaching a boundary point is Cauchy but has no limit in the ball.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness

items.title: Hyperbolic space is complete
items.statement: The Poincare upper half-plane is geodesically and metrically complete.
items.strategy: Parametrize vertical lines and orthogonal semicircles by hyperbolic arclength and show their parameter domains are all R; Hopf–Rinow gives metric completeness.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Example 15.1.6 and Theorem 19.2.1
Bruno Martelli, Hyperbolic Geometry, Chapter 2, Propositions 1.8 and 1.15--1.17 and Corollary 1.9

items.title: Antipodal points on a round sphere have many minimizing geodesics
items.statement: For n≥2, antipodal points of the round n-sphere are joined by infinitely many minimizing half-great-circles.
items.strategy: The explicit great-circle solution gives exp_p(v)=cos|v| p+(sin|v|/|v|)v and shows exp_p is a normal chart on |v|<π. The local distance formula gives distance |v| there; approaching the antipode and using the triangle inequality forces d(p,-p)=π. Every unit tangent direction supplies a distinct half-great-circle of length π, and there are infinitely many directions when n≥2.

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry, Proposition 15.3.1 and Theorem 19.2.1, pp. 117--118 and 141--144

items.title: A complete manifold with zero global injectivity radius
items.statement: A hyperbolic cusp is complete while its pointwise injectivity radii tend to zero, so its global injectivity radius is zero.
items.strategy: Use S^1×R with g=du²+e^{-2u}dθ². The geodesic energy and angular momentum e^{-2u}θ' are constant, so position and velocity remain bounded on each finite time interval; continuation and Hopf–Rinow give completeness. The loop θ↦(θ,u) has length 2πe^{-u} and is noncontractible by projection to S^1. If inj(θ,u)>πe^{-u}, the loop lies in a normal ball diffeomorphic to a Euclidean ball and would be contractible. Hence inj(θ,u)≤πe^{-u}→0.

references.title: Bruno Martelli, Hyperbolic Geometry, Chapter 3 Section 2.2, Example 2.5 and Proposition 2.6, printed pages 58--59

items.title: Hopf–Rinow on a flat cylinder
items.statement: The flat cylinder S¹×R is complete and proper, every two points have a minimizing geodesic, and exponential maps are noninjective.
items.strategy: Lift to R², minimize Euclidean distance among integer translates of one endpoint, and project the chosen segment; closed bounded sets lie in a compact circle times a bounded interval.

references.title: Ben Andrews, Geodesics and Completeness, Theorem 11.5.1 and proof, printed pp. 106--108
